Target takes b : HilbertBasis ι 𝕜 E, a data structure (isometric equivalence with ℓ²(ι)) that implicitly forces completeness and has no [CompleteSpace E]; the text defines the complete orthonormal system as an orthonormal family with dense span in a Hilbert space. Equivalent, but a user holding (b, Orthonormal, dense span) must first build the HilbertBasis (HilbertBasis.mk), so reuse is awkward. Patched target states the text's hypotheses directly (verified).

patch.target: ∀ (𝕜 : Type*) [RCLike 𝕜] (E ι : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E] (b : ι → E), Orthonormal 𝕜 b → (Submodule.span 𝕜 (Set.range b)).topologicalClosure = ⊤ → ∀ x : E, HasSum (fun i => ‖inner 𝕜 (b i) x‖ ^ 2) (‖x‖ ^ 2)
patch.proof:
by
  intro 𝕜 _ E ι _ _ _ b hb hd x
  have hs : ⊤ ≤ (Submodule.span 𝕜 (Set.range b)).topologicalClosure := le_of_eq hd.symm
  have hB : ⇑(HilbertBasis.mk hb hs) = b := HilbertBasis.coe_mk hb hs
  have h := RCLike.hasSum_re 𝕜 ((HilbertBasis.mk hb hs).hasSum_inner_mul_inner x x)
  rw [hB] at h
  have h1 : (fun i => RCLike.re (inner 𝕜 x (b i) * inner 𝕜 (b i) x)) =
      fun i => ‖inner 𝕜 (b i) x‖ ^ 2 := by
    funext i
    rw [← inner_conj_symm x (b i), RCLike.conj_mul, ← RCLike.ofReal_pow, RCLike.ofReal_re]
  rw [h1, inner_self_eq_norm_sq] at h
  exact h

findings.issue: Same issue as parseval_identity_hilbert_basis: target uses the HilbertBasis structure (hidden completeness) while the text speaks of an orthonormal family with dense span. Patched target states the text's hypotheses (verified).

patch.target: ∀ (𝕜 : Type*) [RCLike 𝕜] (E ι : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E] (b : ι → E), Orthonormal 𝕜 b → (Submodule.span 𝕜 (Set.range b)).topologicalClosure = ⊤ → ∀ x : E, HasSum (fun i => (inner 𝕜 (b i) x) • b i) x
patch.proof:
by
  intro 𝕜 _ E ι _ _ _ b hb hd x
  have hs : ⊤ ≤ (Submodule.span 𝕜 (Set.range b)).topologicalClosure := le_of_eq hd.symm
  have hB : ⇑(HilbertBasis.mk hb hs) = b := HilbertBasis.coe_mk hb hs
  have h := (HilbertBasis.mk hb hs).hasSum_repr x
  simp only [HilbertBasis.repr_apply_apply, hB] at h
  exact h

Ad-hoc single-use vocabulary symbols hide structure: ae_eventually_outside, ae_holds_all_indices, ae_ball_average_converges, nat_half_lines, unit_bump_seq, lintegral_seq_sup/liminf, integral_seq, measure_seq, set_seq_*, fn_seq_*, seminorm_definite. Prefer lambda-based reusable forms (ae_holds over a term_function, sup/liminf via binders) and consistent seq_value vs fn_value use; also fn_continuous (MI) vs continuous_map (FA) name the same notion, and `norm` is overloaded for vectors, functionals and operators without carrier.

Lean targets are uniformly sound on the junk-value axis: ENNReal subtraction/ofReal/toReal appear only under finiteness or sign hypotheses (measure_of_difference, lebesgue_measure_of_interval, dilation, egorov, jordan), integrals of possibly non-integrable maps are guarded by Integrable/MemLp hypotheses, and σ-finiteness/completeness hypotheses are present exactly where the hard_negatives show they are needed (Tonelli, Fubini, Radon–Nikodym, product-rectangle, open mapping, closed graph, Riesz representation, adjoint).

statement_en for the many measure-of-arbitrary-subset cards (measure_monotone, subadditivity, continuity, Borel–Cantelli, null unions) omits the outer-measure extension convention that the Japanese text states, so the English reads as a statement about measurable sets only while the Lean claims it for all sets; harmless but inconsistent. The 'named' quota is met at 7/52 and 7/50 only because Tonelli, Minkowski, Borel–Cantelli, Egorov, Bessel, Parseval, Hahn/Jordan decomposition, Cauchy–Schwarz, Neumann series and Riesz lemma are labelled textbook/gap.

Two 'counterexample' cards (continuity_from_above_counterexample, pointwise_limit_integral_counterexample) restate hard_negatives of neighbouring cards and are poor reusable lemmas; hard_negative reasons elsewhere are accurate (all the numeric/counterexample checks I redid hold: Tonelli diagonal 1 vs 0, Fubini π/4 vs -π/4, Phillips c0 in ℓ∞, identity on (F,‖·‖+|φ|), typewriter sequence).
